pages.text:
Mechanical
1. Boat Build:
The hull is a modified version of a Mystic C5000, a 51-foot twin inboard catamaran capable of
running 160 mph. We first scaled it down to a length of 7 ft and then also widened the tunnel by
33% to a width of 16 inches. This scaling was chosen using a series of calculations described in
Jim Russell’s Secrets to Tunnel Boat Design. The process starts with some initial estimates of the
overall sizing of the hull, weight of the boat, trim angle, and top speed. First, the aerodynamic lift
and drag were calculated based on the top speed and tunnel dimensions. The total weight and
aerodynamic lift values then determine how much hydrodynamic lift is necessary. This then
determines how much of the boat will be touching the water, which can be used to calculate
hydrodynamic drag. The drag due to various appendages including the motor, cockpit, etc. is
then calculated. Finally a power requirement is calculated to meet the initial estimated speed
with the estimated weight and sizing. For our boat, we then compared this to the power output
we expected from our powertrain. If we had power to spare, then we could adjust the top speed
to be faster. If we were underpowered, then we could either decrease the top speed or increase
the tunnel width. Another parameter that could be adjusted was the angle of attack which greatly
affected the hulls aerodynamic lift. Through a long iterative process we settled on a length of 7 ft
and a tunnel width of 16 inches.
We manufactured the hull in house using a carbon fiber resin infusion process. We made molds
by bolting together several 3D prints which were then sealed using bondo, primer, and epoxy
paint. Mold release was then applied to prepare the mold for infusion. For the bottom of the boat
we used three layers of 6 oz carbon fiber and two layers for the top. There is a very large hatch
door which will allow easy access to most of the hull. There is also a 10 in by 10 in square deck
door in the front to allow access to the front area. There will be a bulkhead which spans the full
width of the boat halfway between the two access doors. The transom will be reinforced to make
sure it can handle the torque of the rudder. Everything mounted in the boat will be epoxied down
which will also add structure.
This boat is the first the team has built that isn’t intended to carry a person. Previously, all our
unmanned boats were full-size manned boats with an RC system installed. It is also our first nonhydroplane boat, with the exception of last year's displacement vessel. For this reason the hull
design was very thorough.

3. Battery and Payload Trays
Batteries and payload are the largest individual contributors to total weight, which determines the
boat's center of gravity (COG). Adjusting their locations along the boat’s length is the simplest
way to adjust weight distribution, so sliding decks have been designed to allow trays to be bolted
down at different points in the sponsons. The rail is around 18” in length, the battery 7.5”, and
the payload 6”. This leaves only 4.5” of adjustability. However, COG estimates show it lands
around the second step of the sponsons, which is the desired location. Adjustability is low
because of the need for bulkheads near the front of the canopy that act as support for the boat
structure.

   4. Driveline Setup

pages.text:
The driveline consists of everything between the motor and propeller. A shaft coupler is set
screwed down to the motor shaft, and on the other side, the flex shaft is clamped down using a
union nut. A load bearing is set into the motor mounting plate, and the coupler sits against it to
allow the plate to partially relieve thrust loads from the internal motor bearings. A “stuffing
tube” is a brass tube used to guide the flex shaft from the motor and into the stinger. The stuffing
tube end is epoxied to the inside of the transom overhang wall and supported with two guide
plates. A stinger is a shaft mounted to the transom overhang wall that guides the drive shaft and
holds the propeller in place.

Figure 7: Driveline setup with four plates: middle motor support, front motor support, and two stuffing
tube supports

There are different common driveshaft options: flex shaft, wire drive, and solid shaft. Flex shafts
are most flexible because they are multistrand cables, which allows for misalignments, but also
they lose power transfer efficiency due to their lower stiffness. Solid shafts are the opposite
because they are made of solid steel, which provides the greatest efficiency but also requires
much more precise alignment of the motor and stinger. Wire drive is the in-between, being a
single solid spring steel wire that requires tensioning. Flex shaft was ultimately selected for its
successful heritage, accessibility, and ability to absorb small misalignments that would likely
exist, since it was the team’s first time setting up a driveline like this.
Propellers are difficult to nail down on the first try. So, multiple low-cost 2-blade carbon
propellers of varying diameter and pitch were purchased for testing. Larger propellers put a
greater load on the motor and ESC, and smaller ones provide insufficient thrust, so finding the
proper size through testing is critical. From tests, the desired diameter and pitch can be narrowed
down in order to purchase more durable, high-quality propellers.
CCFP MK 5 Adjustable Drives were selected for stingers due to their adjustable length and
orientation, as well as the proper length needed to place the propellers near the transom wall.

3/16” and ¼” propeller shafts were selectable as well, allowing for a greater range of usable
propeller sizes.
5. Rudder Steering
A single, centered rudder from MHZ was selected, particularly suitable for the Mystic model. It
is controlled through dual cables pulled by an AGFRC 74 kg-cm servo.
6. Cooling System
The cooling system consists of two identical water coolant setups for each motor-ESC setup.
One coolant setup consists of a heat exchanger with one raw water pickup line and one closed
loop. Specifically, a Duda Diesel B3-5A heat exchanger has two fluid lines, with one connected
to a closed loop with the ESC, motor, pump, and water reservoir. The other line is connected to a
raw water pickup and outlet to intake and expel raw water along with exchanged heat from the
ESC and motor.
7. Risks and Mitigation
Potential risks include water intake and hull blowover. Water intake is inevitable, and to mitigate
it we plan to have drain holes at the bottom corners of the sponsons. Water leakage and
buoyancy tests will be conducted before running the boat to ensure there are no leaks. After each
testing run, water intake will be checked for. Nearly all components will also be splash proof
and/or water sealed.
Hull blowover is difficult to predict and will cause significant damage to the boat. To prevent
this from ever occurring, all initial tests will run at low, nonplaning speeds. Only after extensive
testing and confidence in understanding the hull’s performance will planing speeds be attempted.
During testing, COG and propellers will be adjusted, ensuring that we have the correct COG
location and the proper sized propeller to load the motors.

pages.text:
Electrical
1. Electrical System Overview
The electrical architecture is organized into two independent voltage domains: a 48V nominal
high-voltage (HV) propulsion system and a 12V low-voltage (LV) auxiliary and control system.
This deliberate separation ensures that a fault on the propulsion side cannot collapse the logic
and safety systems, and that the remote kill switch remains operational under all foreseeable
failure conditions.
The HV system delivers power to two motors through a dual-inverter architecture, each motor
fed by its own dedicated 24V battery pair. The LV system governs all relay switching, circuit
protection, autonomous enable logic, water pump cooling, and RC receiver communication. The
two domains interface only through isolated control signals – no direct electrical connection
exists between the 48V and 12V.

Figure 8: KiCad schematic of the autonomous LV system. Dual inverter channels (Inv1A/1B for M1;
Inv2A/2B for M2), relay logic (K1 kill switch, K2 autonomous enable), RC receiver (Recv1), and HV
battery interfaces (BT1, BT3). Autonomous computing stack excluded

pages.text:
2. High-Voltage Propulsion System
A. Architecture
The HV propulsion system consists of two fully independent drive channels. Each channel
comprises a 48V battery pack (two 24V LiPo packs in series), a dedicated inverter (electronic
speed controller), and a brushless motor. The channels share no common HV rail – each battery,
inverter, and motor set is electrically isolated from the other at the propulsion voltage level. This
means a cell failure, ESC fault, or phase-short on one channel cannot directly propagate to the
other, preserving at least partial propulsion authority. The dual-channel approach also provides
symmetric thrust loading across the hull, which is critical for maintaining heading stability at
competition speeds without relying solely on rudder correction.
B. Ignition System and Remote Kill Switch Integration
The ignition system is the interface between the LV control domain and the HV propulsion
domain. Each ESC has a built-in ignition switch. This switch has been rewired to connect to a
remote relay that will receive a signal from an operator on land. This relay has a roughly fivemile radius to ensure safety.
C. ESC Configuration and Throttle Control
The Cobra HV ESC is selected for its compatibility with the 48V system voltage, its highresolution PWM throttle input, and its data logging capabilities via Castle Link USB. Data
logging records voltage, current, RPM, throttle percentage, and temperature throughout each run,
providing the telemetry needed to tune motor and propeller selection between heats.
The ESC accepts a standard 50Hz PWM signal on the PWM_IN line from the autonomous
controller. The onboard BEC produces a regulated +5V supply that powers the Hall-effect sensor
harness and is available to the autonomous stack as a backup logic supply. Temperature
monitoring through TEMP_IN enables automatic thermal rollback before the ESC or motor
reaches damaging temperatures – essential in a sealed marine enclosure where airflow is limited.

Figure 9: HV propulsion enclosure (Model EE-ADM-002). Upper: dual Turnigy 16,000mAh 48V LiPo
packs in weatherproof housing with high-voltage warning labeling. Lower: Castle Creations Cobra HV
ESC, matched brushless motor, rotary isolator switch, bus bar distribution, and multimeter for field
voltage verification.

3. Low-Voltage Auxiliary and Control System
A. 12V Logic Battery
A 12V 7.0Ah sealed lead-acid (SLA/AGM) battery provides the LV supply rail. SLA chemistry
was chosen for its tolerance to partial state-of-charge cycling, its flat discharge curve under light
loads, and its safety in a marine environment — no venting, no thermal runaway risk, and no
special charging supervision required during competition operation. The 7.0Ah capacity is
substantially oversized relative to the quiescent draw of the relay coils, RC receiver, and pump
motors, providing multi-hour endurance and significant tolerance to voltage sag during relay
switching transients. A panel-mount digital voltmeter on the enclosure face allows operators to
verify the LV battery state at a glance before and during competition.
B. Relay Logic
Relays perform the critical switching and gating functions in the LV system [See Figure 8 for
implementation].
C. Fuse Block and Circuit Protection
A six-position blade fuse block distributes 12V power independently to each LV load. Individual
fusing means a fault in any single circuit – such as a stalled pump motor or a chafed wire short –
blows only that branch's fuse without affecting relay logic, the kill switch path, or any other
subsystem. Fuse ratings are selected above each circuit's expected steady-state draw but below
the wire ampacity, ensuring the fuse protects the wiring before a damaging temperature is
reached.
D. LV Enclosure: Physical Implementation
The LV enclosure places the dual 12V 7.0Ah battery cells on the right side for weight ballast
contribution, the DIN-rail relay bank on the left for easy relay swap, and the six-position fuse
block centrally for maximum field accessibility. All wiring uses color-coded stranded wire with
ferrule-terminated ends: red for 12V positive, black for ground, blue for switched outputs, and
yellow for relay coil signal lines. A push-button power switch and digital voltmeter are panel-

pages.text:
Figure 11: Cube Orange

The Cube Orange serves as the central processing unit of the autonomous system, running
ArduRover firmware and coordinating all actuation, navigation, and fail-safe logic. It interfaces
with every subsystem on the vessel, receiving positional data from the GPS module, sending
PWM commands to the ESCs and rudder servo, and monitoring radio link status to trigger safety
responses when needed.
2. Autonomous Navigation

Figure 12: Waypoint navigation mapping software

Waypoint navigation is managed natively through ArduRover's auto mode, with mission
planning and upload handled via Mission Planner ground control software. The autopilot
executes heading and speed control using tuned PID controllers that govern cross-track error
correction and throttle response. To adapt to varying race day conditions, including wave height,
wind drift, and payload variation, the team developed a set of LUA scripts that dynamically load
pre-tuned PID profiles without requiring firmware modification. This provides operational
flexibility between runs and allows the team to respond to changing water conditions without
reflashing or recalibrating the autopilot.

pages.text:
3. RTK Positioning

Figure 13: Here 3+ GNSS module

Without RTK correction, the Here 3+ GNSS module provides approximately 5 meters of circular
error possible. While sufficient for general navigation, this level of accuracy introduces
meaningful deviation over a multi-waypoint race course. With the RTK4 base station providing
differential corrections via radio link, positional accuracy improves to under 5 centimeters. The
base station acts as a fixed ground reference, continuously broadcasting carrier-phase corrections
to the rover receiver on the vessel. This level of precision is critical for consistent waypoint
tracking and repeatable course execution.
4. Radio System

Figures 14 and 15: Receiver and transmitter module

The Radiomaster ELRS True Diversity receiver is bound to the ELRS transmitter module,
providing a reliable control link with a tested range exceeding 1.5 miles. A dedicated channel on
the transmitter is mapped to the kill switch function, giving the safety operator an immediate
manual disarm capability at all times. Fail-safe behavior, consisting of throttle cut and hold
mode, is configured directly in the autopilot firmware and triggers automatically on signal loss.
This means the vessel does not require operator intervention to reach a safe state if the radio link
is interrupted.

base station acts as a fixed ground reference, continuously broadcasting carrier-phase corrections
to the rover receiver on the vessel. This level of precision is critical for consistent waypoint
tracking and repeatable course execution.

   4. Radio System




                         Figures 14 and 15: Receiver and transmitter module

  The Radiomaster ELRS True Diversity receiver is bound to the ELRS transmitter module,
providing a reliable control link with a tested range exceeding 1.5 miles. A dedicated channel on
the transmitter is mapped to the kill switch function, giving the safety operator an immediate
manual disarm capability at all times. Fail-safe behavior, consisting of throttle cut and hold
mode, is configured directly in the autopilot firmware and triggers automatically on signal loss.
This means the vessel does not require operator intervention to reach a safe state if the radio link
is interrupted.

pages.text:
5. Companion Computing

Figure 16: NVIDIA Jetson

An NVIDIA Jetson is integrated as a companion computer, communicating with the Cube
Orange via MAVLink over serial. The Jetson handles computationally intensive tasks, including
enhanced path planning and sensor fusion, offloading these from the autopilot and providing
capacity for future capability expansion. Importantly, the Jetson is non-critical to the core
autopilot function. If it fails or is disconnected, the Cube Orange continues operating fully
autonomously with no degradation to basic waypoint navigation.
6. Software Development & LUA Scripting
LUA scripts were developed to interface with ArduRover's scripting API, enabling dynamic
parameter updates at runtime. Scripts are loaded from the autopilot's SD card and executed on
boot or triggered by channel input. This allows the team to switch between tuning profiles for
different wave and speed environments without modifying firmware. The scripting approach
keeps the core autopilot firmware untouched while giving the team full control over behavior
customization, reducing the risk of introducing bugs into the flight stack itself.

   7. Testing Process

pages.text:
Figure 17: Testing using an RC car

Prior to hull assembly, the complete autonomous electronics stack, including the Cube Orange,
ESCs, GPS, radio, and LUA scripts, was validated using a ground vehicle. This approach
confirmed waypoint following behavior, PID response, and scripting functionality in a real
dynamic environment without water exposure risk, serving as a proof of concept for the software
architecture. The car-based testing phase allowed the team to iterate rapidly on tuning and script
development in a low-risk setting. Water-based testing then validated ESC and servo
performance under load, RTK lock acquisition time, ELRS link quality at operational distances,
and full autonomous waypoint mission completion from start to finish.
8. Risk Identification & Mitigation
The autonomous system introduces several risks that were identified during the design phase and
addressed through hardware selection, software configuration, and operational procedures.
Radio signal loss is the highest-consequence risk for an autonomous vessel. If the radio link is
interrupted, ArduRover's built-in fail-safe automatically cuts throttle and enters hold mode
within a configured timeout. This is the primary safety response and requires no operator action.
The system reaches a safe state on its own.
RTK correction loss is a degraded-performance scenario rather than a failure. If the RTK4 base
station link is interrupted, the vessel falls back to standalone Here 3+ GPS at approximately 5meter accuracy. Autonomous missions continue with degraded positional precision rather than
failing outright, allowing the vessel to complete its course with reduced but still functional
navigation.

pages.text:
Jetson failure has no impact on the core autonomous function. The Cube Orange operates fully
autonomously without the companion computer, with no degradation to basic waypoint
navigation.
Loss of situational awareness by the safety crew is mitigated by a strobe LED mounted on the
hull. The LED communicates the vessel's current behavioral state in real time, allowing
observers to determine at a glance whether the boat is in manual control, autonomous operation,
or fail-safe mode.
Finally, collision or out-of-bounds behavior is addressed through a kill switch on a dedicated
ELRS channel, allowing the safety operator to immediately disarm the vessel at any time.
Combined with the automatic fail-safe, this creates two independent layers of safety, one
operator-triggered and one autonomous, ensuring the vessel can be stopped reliably under any
failure scenario.
